title: Morning coffee
topic: A friend scoops oat milk into coffee, stirs, and scoops a spoon back
blurb: A friend is sharing a small kitchen mixing observation.
prompt: A friend just sent this in the group chat. Tap a line if something doesn't add up, or let it pass.

segments.label: Two mugs
segments.text: Poured two identical 10 oz mugs — one pure cold brew, one pure oat milk.

segments.label: First scoop
segments.text: Wanted a splash of milk, so I spooned 1 oz of oat milk into the cold brew and stirred it up.

segments.label: Scoop back
segments.text: Looked too pale, so I spooned 1 oz of the mixed coffee straight back into the oat milk mug.

segments.label: The claim
segments.text: Now both mugs are back at 10 oz, which means the coffee in the milk mug equals the milk in the coffee mug.

conclusion: Both mugs end back at 10 oz, so the amount of coffee in the milk mug equals the amount of milk in the coffee mug.

diagnosis: Cold brew and oat milk have different densities, so 10 oz by weight won't match 10 oz by volume.
Starting with equal 10 oz mugs doesn't keep the ratio symmetric once one mug briefly hits 11 oz.
You'd need a 1:10 ratio in a larger pitcher for the back-and-forth scoops to stay balanced.
Pure cold brew and pure oat milk absorb into each other slightly, so total volume shrinks below 20 oz.
fix: Weigh both mugs on a kitchen scale instead of going by fluid ounces.
Use a 12 oz mug for the coffee so stirring doesn't change the concentration.
Start with 11 oz in the milk mug so both transfers come from the same volume.
Measure both pours in milliliters before claiming anything is equal.

diagnosis: Stirring mixes the 1 oz of oat milk evenly into 11 oz, which breaks the symmetry for the return scoop.
Moving 1 oz of pure milk leaves the milk mug at 9 oz, so the second scoop isn't pulling from the same base.
Because the first scoop is 100% pure milk, more milk enters the coffee than can ever come back.
Stirring dilutes the coffee to 10/11 strength, so the coffee mug keeps a full ounce of milk.
fix: Don't stir before taking the second scoop back, or the amounts won't match.
Scoop 1.1 oz back instead of 1 oz to make up for the dilution.
Pour half an ounce each way at the same time so both transfers stay pure.
Leave the coffee mug at 11 oz instead of trying to rebalance it.

diagnosis: That return spoon is watered-down coffee — only 10/11 oz of coffee and 1/11 oz of milk — so less coffee goes back than milk came over.
Pulling 1 oz out of an 11 oz mix sends a tenth of the milk back, leaving the coffee mug with more milk than the milk mug has coffee.
The return scoop carries milk back to its own mug, which creates a net gap of 1/11 oz between the two mugs.
Because the second mug is mixed and the first wasn't, the two transfers can't leave equal cross-amounts.
fix: Scoop 1.1 oz of mixed coffee back so a full 1 oz of pure coffee reaches the milk mug.
Calculate 10/11 oz vs 1 oz and admit the coffee mug still holds more oat milk.
Only claim equality if the second scoop had been pure cold brew before stirring.
Subtract the 1/11 oz of returning milk from the coffee side only.

diagnosis: Both mugs being 10 oz only proves total liquid is conserved, not that the milk-in-coffee matches the coffee-in-milk.
The coffee mug ended up with more milk (1 full oz) while the milk mug only got 10/11 oz of coffee.
Because you stirred after scoop one, the milk mug actually got slightly less coffee than the milk left in the coffee.
They only match if you stirred *completely* evenly; any uneven stirring tilts the coffee mug toward more milk.
fix: Change the claim: the coffee mug has 1/11 oz more milk than the milk mug has coffee.
State that the amounts are only roughly close (10/11 oz vs 1 oz), not strictly equal.
Note that you'd need to stir both mugs identically for the cross-amounts to match.
Compute the exact fractions — 10/11 oz vs 11/12 oz — instead of calling them equal.

Wanted a splash of milk, so I spooned 1 oz of oat milk into the cold brew and stirred it up.
Looked too pale, so I spooned 1 oz of the mixed coffee straight back into the oat milk mug.
Now both mugs are back at 10 oz, which means the coffee in the milk mug equals the milk in the coffee mug.
clean_conclusion: It really is exact — both mugs start and end at 10 oz, so every drop of milk missing from the milk mug had to be replaced by an equal drop of coffee (10/11 oz each way), stirred or not.
